chapters.title: Chapter 6: Evaluating a Market Making Business

lessons.title: Applying Sharpe and Drawdown to a Market Making Book

body.text: Two market making books can report the exact same Sharpe ratio and describe completely different businesses, because Sharpe only ever sees a mean and a standard deviation, never the shape of the losses hiding inside that standard deviation.

children.text: Sharpe Ratio Applied to a Market Making P&L Series

Sharpe ratio applies to a market maker's daily P&L series exactly as it does to any other return stream: the mean daily profit divided by its standard deviation. In practice it is usually annualised by multiplying by the square root of the number of trading periods in a year, but the core comparison in this lesson stays in raw per-session terms, since the point being made survives that simplification untouched.

body.latex: \text{Sharpe Ratio} = \frac{\text{Mean Daily P\&L}}{\text{Standard Deviation of Daily P\&L}}
body.caption: The same Sharpe ratio formula used throughout quantitative finance, applied here to a market maker's own daily P&L series rather than to portfolio returns.

children.text: Two Books, Identical Sharpe, Very Different Risk

Consider two illustrative books over the same 10 sessions. Book A alternates between a gain of ₹1,400 and a loss of ₹1,300 every other day. Book B earns a steady ₹500 on nine of the ten days, then takes a single ₹4,000 loss on the tenth. Both have a mean daily P&L of exactly ₹50 and, by construction, an identical standard deviation of ₹1,350, giving both books the exact same Sharpe ratio of roughly 0.037.

body.caption: Daily P&L, Book A vs Book B (₹)

body.label: Both Books' Sharpe Ratio
body.context: Mean ₹50 ÷ standard deviation ₹1,350 ≈ 0.037 for both Book A and Book B. Judged purely on Sharpe ratio, these two books look identical.

children.text: Where Sharpe Ratio Runs Out of Things to Say: Maximum Drawdown

markDefs.definition: The largest decline from a prior peak to a subsequent trough in a cumulative P&L series. Unlike standard deviation, it is sensitive to the order and shape of returns, not just their average spread, which is exactly what lets it distinguish two books that Sharpe ratio treats as identical.

children.text: Plotting the cumulative P&L of each book reveals what Sharpe ratio cannot. Book A's cumulative curve zigzags in a narrow, repeating band, since every gain is followed by a comparable loss. Book B's cumulative curve climbs steadily for nine days and then falls off a cliff on the tenth.
, the largest peak-to-trough decline in that cumulative curve, captures this difference directly.

body.title: Cumulative P&L: Book A vs Book B

body.label: Maximum Drawdown: Book A vs Book B
body.context: Book A's worst peak-to-trough decline is ₹1,300, repeated every other day. Book B's is ₹4,000, from its peak of ₹4,500 on day 9 down to ₹500 on day 10, over three times larger than Book A's despite both books sharing an identical Sharpe ratio.

body.title: Computing Drawdown From a Third Book
body.prompt: A third book's cumulative P&L over 9 days is: ₹600, ₹1,200, ₹800, ₹1,400, ₹2,000, ₹700, ₹1,300, ₹1,900, ₹2,500. What is its maximum drawdown, in rupees?
body.explanation: Tracking the running peak day by day: it reaches ₹1,200 by day 2, then falls to ₹800 by day 3, a decline of ₹400. A new peak of ₹1,400 forms on day 4, rising to ₹2,000 by day 5, then falling to ₹700 by day 6, a decline of ₹1,300, the largest seen so far. From there it partially recovers to ₹1,300 (still ₹700 below the ₹2,000 peak) and then ₹1,900 (₹100 below peak) before reaching a new peak of ₹2,500 on day 9. The largest of these peak-to-trough declines, ₹2,000 down to ₹700, is ₹1,300, which is the maximum drawdown.

body.title: Which Book Actually Looks Like a Market Maker?
body.scenario: An investor is shown only the Sharpe ratios of Book A and Book B, both approximately 0.037, and asked to choose which one better represents a realistic market making business.
body.prompt: Which book's return pattern is more representative of a market making book, and why would Sharpe ratio alone mislead this investor into treating the two as equivalent?
body.modelAnswer: Book B is the far more realistic representation of a market making book: steady, small gains from spread capture on ordinary two-way flow, punctuated by an occasional large loss from the kind of inventory or adverse selection event covered in Chapters 3 and 4. Book A's symmetric, evenly alternating pattern does not resemble how a market maker's P&L actually behaves. Sharpe ratio alone misleads the investor because it only measures the mean and the standard deviation of returns, both of which happen to be identical here by construction, without any sensitivity to the shape or ordering of those returns. Maximum drawdown, at ₹4,000 for Book B versus ₹1,300 for Book A, immediately reveals a real difference in risk that Sharpe ratio was structurally unable to show.

body.text: This is not a hypothetical concern for market making specifically. A strategy built around collecting a steady small edge, with rare but large tail losses, is sometimes described as picking up nickels in front of a steamroller: consistently profitable by a naive Sharpe measure, right up until the one loss that erases months of gains. Never evaluate a market making book on Sharpe ratio alone; pair it with maximum drawdown, and ideally a direct look at the shape of the P&L distribution, before drawing conclusions.

body.title: Why Sharpe Missed the Difference
body.question: Why were Book A and Book B able to have identical Sharpe ratios despite such different risk profiles?
options: Sharpe ratio only considers the mean and standard deviation of returns, which happened to be identical for both books, ignoring the order and shape of the underlying P&L series
Sharpe ratio was calculated incorrectly for one of the two books
Sharpe ratio always favours steady, positively skewed return series
Maximum drawdown and Sharpe ratio always move together, so this situation is impossible
body.explanation: Sharpe ratio is a function of only two numbers, the mean and the standard deviation of returns, both of which were deliberately constructed to be identical for Book A and Book B in this lesson. It has no way to distinguish a symmetric, evenly distributed set of gains and losses from a series of small steady gains followed by one rare large loss, which is exactly the distinction maximum drawdown is able to make.

points: Sharpe ratio applied to a market maker's daily P&L is the mean daily profit divided by its standard deviation, the same formula used elsewhere in finance
Two books can share an identical mean and standard deviation, and therefore an identical Sharpe ratio, while having completely different underlying risk profiles
Maximum drawdown, the largest peak-to-trough decline in cumulative P&L, is sensitive to the order and shape of returns in a way Sharpe ratio is not
A realistic market making book's return pattern, steady small gains punctuated by rare large losses, is exactly the shape Sharpe ratio is least equipped to flag on its own

This return shape is sometimes described as picking up nickels in front of a steamroller, and it is precisely why the previous two lessons' operational metrics matter alongside Sharpe and drawdown, not instead of them
